title: Mother witnessed police shoot son in Exeter after calling 911 for help: Relative
article: An Exeter man was fatally shot by police after his mother called 911 to get him help, a family member tells The London Free Press.

Diane Vanderwal watched as Huron OPP officers fired six times at her son, Wade Vanderwal, outside their home at 65 Simcoe St. in Exeter, according to an account shared by the grieving mother's niece, Jennifer Whaling.
"The last thing Aunt Diane has seen of him was him on the ground after he'd been shot," Whaling said Friday.

Ontario's police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit (SIU), says it's probing the actions of two OPP officers in the death of Vanderwal, 44, who they say was armed with an axe when he was shot Tuesday night.
Wade Vanderwal, who had struggled with mental-health issues since he was a child, had told his mother that the army was coming before locking her out of the house, Whaling said.

The distraught mother went across the street to a neighbour's house to ask for help and call police. OPP officers and firefighters soon arrived, but Vanderwal had barricaded the door, prompting them to break it down, Whaling said.

The SIU says Vanderwal came outside the house armed with an axe, prompting two officers to shoot him multiple times. He was later pronounced dead at South Huron Hospital in Exeter, a town of roughly 4,500 that's located 48 kilometres north of London, in Huron County.
"She saw everything. She was right across the street," Whaling said of her aunt.
"So my aunt feels huge guilt because she's the one who called for help."
The SIU says police and firefighters were called to a Simcoe Street address for a fire call. It's unclear whether emergency crews found any evidence of a fire.

A Huron County OPP spokesperson declined to say whether police were responding to a mental-health call, citing the ongoing investigation. The spokesperson also wouldn't confirm how many shots were fired.

One of three children, Vanderwal hadn't worked in "many years" and had lived with his mom since his mid-20s after returning from a stint out west, Whaling said, adding multiple strokes had affected her cousin's speech and thought processing.
Neighbours described him as a quiet man who kept to himself.
"I can't figure out why it happened," next-door neighbour Everett Chisholm said.
Bill Thistle, who lives across the street, described Vanderwal as a friendly neighbour who regularly walked around the area, stopping to chat in front of his home sometimes.
The accusation that Vanderwal charged at police with an axe is out of character, Thistle added. "It seems strange."
On the night of the shooting, Thistle said, he was leaving his home just as fire trucks were on the scene, including what he believed to be the fire chief's pickup truck.

His wife Rhona, who was home at the time, saw two police cruisers stop directly in front of their Simcoe Street home. She saw a male and a female officer rush down the street, and quickly heard several shots echoing through the neighbourhood, Thistle said.

Court records show Vanderwal doesn't have any criminal convictions. A mischief charge against him was withdrawn in March 2016 after he completed a direct accountability program, a process that allows cases to be resolved through a letter of apology, charitable donation or paying restitution.
Vanderwal's family hasn't been able to plan a funeral because investigators have yet to return his body, Whaling said.
"(We) haven't been able to say a proper goodbye to him. You need a little bit of closure," she said.
An SIU spokesperson said a post-mortem was completed in London on Thursday.
Despite lingering questions about the way the OPP handled the incident, the family doesn't blame police, Whaling said.
"It's really more frustrating with the system and not just police," she said.
